Model Calibration, Selection, and Ensembles

Source: vignettes/model-calibration-and-selection.Rmd
model-calibration-and-selection.Rmd

Overview

Choosing the right model — and its hyperparameters — is critical for mortality forecasting. mortensor provides a unified calibration framework that:

  1. Searches over Tucker3 ranks (RA,RB,RC)(R_A, R_B, R_C) and time-series methods
  2. Calibrates all competing models (Lee-Carter, FDM, StMoMo, ARIMA, ETS, RWD)
  3. Evaluates on a held-out period using proper scoring rules
  4. Builds inverse-MASE or NNLS ensemble weights
  5. Returns a mort_calibration object ready for forecast()

Available models

Model name Function Description
tucker3_coda tucker3_coda_forecast() Tucker3 on CLR-transformed death shares
tucker3_direct tucker3_direct_forecast() Tucker3 on log(mx) directly
lee_carter lca_forecast() Lee-Carter (via demography)
fdm fdm_forecast() Functional demographic model
stmomo stmomo_forecast() StMoMo APC/CBD (via StMoMo)
arima arima_forecast() Per-series auto.arima on log(mx)
ets ets_forecast() Per-series ETS (damped) on log(mx)
rwd rwd_forecast() Per-series random walk with drift

Models requiring optional packages (demography, StMoMo) are silently skipped if the package is not installed.

The calibrate() function

The main entry point for model selection is calibrate():

library(mortensor)
data(example_mortality)

# Smooth first
sm <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",
                       covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))

# Calibrate with defaults
cal <- calibrate(sm)
print(cal)
summary(cal)

Key parameters 

cal <- calibrate(
  data           = sm,                  # mort_data (smoothed recommended)
  models         = c("tucker3_coda",    # which models to evaluate
                     "tucker3_direct",
                     "lee_carter", "fdm",
                     "ets", "arima", "rwd"),
  holdout_years  = NULL,                # explicit holdout years (overrides frac)
  holdout_frac   = 0.2,                # fraction of years for holdout
  ensemble       = TRUE,               # build ensemble from top models
  ensemble_top_k = 3L,                 # how many models in ensemble
  config         = mort_config()        # optional configuration object
)

What happens inside calibrate()

  1. Train/test split: The last holdout_frac of years (or holdout_years) are withheld for evaluation.

  2. Smoothing: If data$smoothed is FALSE, smooth_mortality() is called automatically.

  3. Tucker3 calibration: calibrate_tucker3() searches over rank combinations for both CoDa and Direct variants, selecting the best (RA,RB,RC,ts_method)(R_A, R_B, R_C, \text{ts\_method}).

  4. Other model calibration: calibrate_all_models() evaluates Lee-Carter, FDM, StMoMo, RWD, ARIMA, and ETS via expanding-window CV.

  5. Holdout comparison: compare_models() runs every calibrated model on the training set, forecasts into the holdout period, and scores with combined MASE (0.7 cell-level + 0.3 group-trend).

  6. Ensemble construction: The top-kk models are combined using inverse-MASE weights (or optionally NNLS stacking).

Tucker3 rank selection in detail

Cross-validation (recommended)

Rolling-origin CV (rank_selection = "cv") trains on expanding windows and evaluates on the next hh years:

calib_coda <- calibrate_tucker3(
  mx_array       = sm$mx,
  years          = sm$years,
  ages           = sm$ages,
  method         = "coda",
  rank_selection = "cv",
  h_val          = 3,           # 3-year validation windows
  min_train      = 12           # at least 12 training years
)

# Result contains the optimal configuration
str(calib_coda)
# $R_A       : 3
# $R_B       : 2
# $R_C       : 2
# $ts_method : "ets"
# $cv_score   : 0.847

The CV procedure:

  1. For each rank combination, fit Tucker3 on years [1,T0][1, T_0], forecast hh steps, score against held-out truth using the chosen cv_metric.
  2. Roll forward: train on [1,T0+1][1, T_0+1], forecast, score.
  3. Average scores across origins.
  4. Select ranks with lowest average score.
  5. Given best ranks, compare ts_method ∈\in{arima, ets, rwd}.

By default, the scoring metric is cell-level MASE (cv_metric = "mase"). You can also use "mase_combined" (0.7 × cell + 0.3 × trend) or "mase_trend" (trend only). See the CV metric selection section below.

Information criteria (fast)

For quick exploration, BIC or AIC can select ranks without refitting time-series models:

calib_bic <- calibrate_tucker3(
  mx_array       = sm$mx,
  years          = sm$years,
  ages           = sm$ages,
  method         = "coda",
  rank_selection = "bic"        # or "aic"
)

BIC penalises model complexity more than AIC, favouring lower ranks. This is fast (seconds vs minutes for CV) but does not account for forecast performance.

Direct comparison of selection methods 

# Both methods
calib_cv  <- calibrate_tucker3(sm$mx, sm$years, sm$ages,
                                method = "coda", rank_selection = "cv")
calib_bic <- calibrate_tucker3(sm$mx, sm$years, sm$ages,
                                method = "coda", rank_selection = "bic")

cat(sprintf("CV  ranks: (%d, %d, %d) — MASE: %.3f\n",
            calib_cv$R_A, calib_cv$R_B, calib_cv$R_C, calib_cv$cv_score))
cat(sprintf("BIC ranks: (%d, %d, %d) — BIC: %.1f\n",
            calib_bic$R_A, calib_bic$R_B, calib_bic$R_C, calib_bic$ic_value))

Calibrating non-tensor models

calibrate_all_models() handles the remaining model zoo:

calib_all <- calibrate_all_models(
  mx_array  = sm$mx,
  pop_array = sm$pop,        # population exposure (optional for some models)
  years     = sm$years,
  ages      = sm$ages,
  groups    = sm$groups,
  h_val     = 4,             # 4-year validation windows
  n_origins = 4,             # 4 rolling origins
  width     = 5              # 5-year age groups
)

# Inspect per-model calibration results
names(calib_all)
# [1] "lc" "fdm" "stmomo" "rwd" "arima" "ets"

# Each entry has model-specific parameters + cv_score
calib_all$lc
# $adjust     : "dt"
# $order      : 6
# $method     : "arima"
# $cv_score    : 0.912

calib_all$ets
# $damped     : TRUE
# $cv_score    : 1.034

CV metric selection

By default, cross-validation selects hyperparameters using cell-level MASE (cv_metric = "mase"). The cv_metric parameter lets you choose an alternative scoring function applied to all models during calibration:

cv_metric Function Description
"mase" compute_mase_array() Cell-level MASE (default)
"mase_combined" compute_mase_combined() 0.7 × cell + 0.3 × trend MASE
"mase_trend" compute_mase_group_trend() Group-trend MASE only

Using "mase_combined" aligns calibration with the metric used for final model ranking in compare_models(), which can lead to more consistent selections:

# Calibrate Tucker3 using combined MASE
calib_combined <- calibrate_tucker3(
  mx_array  = sm$mx,
  years     = sm$years,
  ages      = sm$ages,
  method    = "coda",
  cv_metric = "mase_combined"
)

# The top-level calibrate() passes cv_metric to all models
cal <- calibrate(sm, cv_metric = "mase_combined")

Model comparison and scoring

The holdout evaluation uses compare_models() internally. The comparison data.table is stored in the calibration object:

cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)

# View the comparison table
print(cal$comparison)
#              model      mase mase_trend mase_combined
# 1:    Tucker3-CoDa  0.847     0.721        0.809
# 2:  Tucker3-Direct  0.891     0.756        0.851
# 3:      Lee-Carter  0.923     0.812        0.890
# 4:             FDM  0.967     0.845        0.930
# 5:      ETS-Damped  1.034     0.923        0.991
# 6: ARIMA-perSeries  1.089     0.967        1.052
# 7:             RWD  1.123     1.001        1.087

# The combined MASE is 0.7 * cell + 0.3 * trend

The combined MASE balances cell-level accuracy (capturing age-group patterns) with group-trend accuracy (capturing overall decline rates). This prevents selecting a model that is accurate on average but misses important trends.

Visualise model comparison 

plot(cal)  # bar chart of MASE by model

Ensemble construction

Inverse-MASE weighting (default)

The top-kk models are weighted inversely proportional to their MASE:

wi=1/MASEi∑j=1k1/MASEj w_i = \frac{1/\text{MASE}_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{k} 1/\text{MASE}_j} 

# Inspect ensemble
cat("Ensemble members:", cal$ensemble_names, "\n")
cat("Weights:", round(cal$ensemble_weights, 3), "\n")

# Example output:
# Ensemble members: Tucker3-CoDa Tucker3-Direct Lee-Carter
# Weights: 0.412 0.321 0.267

Controlling ensemble membership 

# Only Tucker3 models in ensemble
cal_t3 <- calibrate(sm,
                    models = c("tucker3_coda", "tucker3_direct"),
                    ensemble = TRUE, ensemble_top_k = 2)

# No ensemble — use single best model
cal_single <- calibrate(sm, ensemble = FALSE)
cat("Best single model:", cal_single$best_model, "\n")

# Larger ensemble
cal_big <- calibrate(sm, ensemble = TRUE, ensemble_top_k = 5)

NNLS stacking (advanced)

If the nnls package is installed, non-negative least-squares can determine weights by minimising holdout forecast error directly:

# NNLS is used automatically if nnls is installed and ensemble = TRUE
# The method that produces lower holdout MASE (inverse-MASE or NNLS) is kept

Dispatching forecasts

The forecast() method on mort_calibration uses dispatch_forecast() to route to the correct model function:

# forecast() internally calls dispatch_forecast() for each ensemble member,
# then combines using the stored weights
fc <- forecast(cal, h = 10)

# For a single-model calibration, it dispatches directly
fc_single <- forecast(cal_single, h = 10)
cat("Model used:", fc_single$model, "\n")

The dispatch table:

Calibration model Dispatches to
tucker3_coda tucker3_coda_forecast()
tucker3_direct tucker3_direct_forecast()
lee_carter lca_forecast()
fdm fdm_forecast()
stmomo stmomo_forecast()
arima arima_forecast()
ets ets_forecast()
rwd rwd_forecast()

Expanding-window CV for any model

You can run expanding-window cross-validation for any model independently:

cv_result <- cv_expanding_model(
  mx_array  = sm$mx,
  pop_array = sm$pop,
  years     = sm$years,
  ages      = sm$ages,
  groups    = sm$groups,
  model     = "lee_carter",
  h_val     = 4,
  n_origins = 4,
  width     = 5
)

cat("Lee-Carter CV score:", round(cv_result$cv_score, 3), "\n")

Using mort_config for calibration settings

The mort_config object centralises pipeline settings:

cfg <- mort_config(
  forecast_h       = 10L,
  n_sim            = 500L,
  smoothing_method = "gam",
  covid_years      = c(2020L, 2021L, 2022L),
  holdout_train    = 0.8,     # 80% train / 20% holdout
  holdout_test     = 0.2
)

cal <- calibrate(sm, config = cfg)

Complete example: from data to calibrated ensemble 

library(mortensor)
data(example_mortality)

# 1. Smooth
sm <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",
                       covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))

# 2. Calibrate all models with 20% holdout, top-3 ensemble
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2,
                 ensemble = TRUE, ensemble_top_k = 3)

# 3. Inspect results
summary(cal)
plot(cal)

# 4. Check ensemble
cat("Best model:", cal$best_model, "\n")
cat("Ensemble:", paste(cal$ensemble_names, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Weights:", paste(round(cal$ensemble_weights, 3), collapse = ", "), "\n")

# 5. Forecast
fc <- forecast(cal, h = 10)
summary(fc)

# 6. Export calibration details
export(cal, dir = "calibration_results/")

Summary

  • calibrate() is the one-stop function for model selection and ensemble building
  • Tucker3 ranks are selected via CV (accurate) or BIC/AIC (fast)
  • All models are compared on a holdout set using combined MASE
  • Inverse-MASE weighting produces robust ensembles
  • The mort_calibration object plugs directly into forecast(), add_pi(), and export()
